abstract: Diabetic ulcers and peripheral artery disease remain difficult to treat because current treatments cannot regenerate functional and stable blood vessels. The origin of the smooth muscle cell (SMC) support required for vessel stability is unclear. In mouse injury models, we identified a FAP+Pi16+ fibroblast subpopulation that transcriptionally differentiates into arteriolar SMCs via TGFβR1 signaling. Lineage tracing showed that FAP+ fibroblasts give rise to SMCs during de novo arteriole formation. scRNA-seq trajectory analysis combined with dual-recombinase lineage tracing confirmed that FAP+Pi16+ fibroblasts contribute to the arteriolar SMC pool. Ablation of FAP+ fibroblasts disrupted arteriolar assembly and delayed repair. Loss of TGFβR1 impaired SMC generation, whereas pharmacologic activation of TGFβR1 enhanced arteriole formation. Transplantation of FAP+Pi16+ fibroblasts into ischemic limbs restored perfusion and accelerated functional recovery. FAP+Pi16+ fibroblasts are conserved in human diabetic ulcers and acutely injured skin, supporting FAP+Pi16+ fibroblast-to-SMC differentiation as a route to arteriole regeneration in ischemic disease.
